newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S TELKOM HEADS FOR AFRICAN CABLE SHOWDOWN.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S TELKOM HEADS FOR AFRICAN CABLE SHOWDOWN.

text.p: South African utility Telkom is heading for a clash with a giant telecommunications project over plans to improve Africa's links to a global web of communications cables, an industry figure said on Thursday.
Telkom recently announced plans to build a cable hugging the coast of Africa from Cape Town to Senegal that could cost up to $400 million.
But the plan clashes with the Africa One project to ring the entire continent with an undersea cable 20,000 miles long that will connect 41 countries at a cost of around $1.4 billion.
Telkom says there is only room for one cable up the western and southern coasts of Africa.
"I doubt whether there is any feasibilty in having two cables in the same area," Johan Meyer, head of Telkom's global cable business, told Reuters.
Telkom has already signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on its cable, called Sat-3, with Gabon TIG, Ghana Telecommunications and Senegal's Sonatel.
Other countries are expected to follow with industry sources saying at least four more Western and Southern African operators are expected to sign MOUs over the next few weeks.
Telkom has held talks with Africa One to seek an agreement.
Africa One, which was first backed by U.S. firm AT&T Corp working with France's Alactel Alsthom Cie Generale d'Electrictie , aims to become an incorporated company.

Telkom says Sat-3 could fit into this by becoming one segment of the ring -- physically forming part of the circle but operating independently. The rest of Africa One could then also be run independently as a singular entity or several segments.
But talks have made little progress.
"We have not discontinued discussions altogether. At this point in time the ball is in the court of Africa One. We are open to discussions," Meyer said.

One possible obstacle to Telkom's plans faded in April. As part of its privatisation process the South African government sold a 30 percent stake in the concern to a consortium of U.S.-based SBC Communications Inc and Telekom Malaysia.
AT&T is merging with SBC in a move that could give it an uncomfortable strategic interest in both competing cables.
However, the difficult was neatly resolved when AT&T sold its undersea cables business to U.S. industrial firm Tyco International Ltd .

Another cable, called SAT-2, already exists linking Cape Town to communications nodes in the Canary Islands and Madeira. Meyer said Sat-2's capacity was rapidly filling as telecommunications on the continent boom.
The amount of capacity used by the Internet alone is doubling every four to six months, he said.
"We feel that there is such commercial opportunity between Senegal and Southern Africa that there is demand and need for this," he said.
Another alluring prospect is a possible link between two enormous cables currently being built to the north of Africa.

One will sweep from Portugal to Senegal and on to South America, while the other will descend from Germany, through Southern Europe, the Middle East, India, South East Asia, Korea and finally to Japan.
Sat-2 has only a 40th of the capacity of these monster linkages, while Sat-3's newer technology will be much more compatible.
